title: Time, days, and schedules
title_target: なんじですか — Nanji desu ka
goal: Tell the hour and the minutes, ask the time, name the days of the week, and explain opening hours or a schedule with ～から～まで.
bekal: name the seven days of the week
use the ます form for everyday activities
make a simple appointment with someone

dialogs.title: 会話 1 — What time is class?
dialogs.intro: Ani asks a friend about the class schedule. Notice the pattern ～から～まで repeating over several lines.

lines.speaker: アニ:
lines.text: [すみません|Sumimasen]、[いま|ima] [なんじですか|nanji desu ka]。
lines.id: Excuse me, what time is it now?

lines.speaker: たなか:
lines.text: [はちじはんです|Hachi-ji han desu]。

lines.speaker: アニ:
lines.text: [クラスは|Kurasu wa] [なんじからですか|nanji kara desu ka]。
lines.id: What time does the class start?

lines.speaker: たなか:
lines.text: [くじから|Ku-ji kara] [じゅういちじまでです|jūichi-ji made desu]。

lines.speaker: アニ:
lines.text: [やすみは|Yasumi wa] [ありますか|arimasu ka]。

lines.speaker: たなか:
lines.text: [はい|Hai]、[じゅうじから|jū-ji kara] [じゅうじじゅうごふんまで|jū-ji jūgo-fun made] [やすみます|yasumimasu]。
lines.id: Yes, we take a break from ten to ten fifteen.
lines.literal: yes, ten-o'clock — from — ten-o'clock-fifteen-minutes — until — rest.

lines.speaker: アニ:
lines.text: [ごごの|Gogo no] [クラスも|kurasu mo] [ありますか|arimasu ka]。

lines.speaker: たなか:
lines.text: [かようびと|Kayōbi to] [もくようびだけです|mokuyōbi dake desu]。

lines.speaker: アニ:
lines.text: [にちようびは|Nichiyōbi wa] [やすみですか|yasumi desu ka]。

lines.speaker: たなか:
lines.text: [はい|Hai]、[どようびと|doyōbi to] [にちようびは|nichiyōbi wa] [やすみです|yasumi desu]。
lines.id: Yes, Saturday and Sunday are days off.
lines.literal: yes, Saturday — and — Sunday — as-for — day-off — is.

lines.speaker: アニ:
lines.text: [わかりました|Wakarimashita]。[ありがとうございます|Arigatō gozaimasu]。

notes: **なんじ = what time, なんぷん = how many minutes.** Notice that hours use the counter **じ (時)** and minutes use **ふん/ぷん (分)** — two different counters that can't be swapped.
**はん = half**, and it comes after the hour: はちじはん = 8:30. It's much more common than はちじさんじゅっぷん, although both are correct.
**だけ = only**, placed **after** the word it limits: かようびだけ = only Tuesday. Unlike English, where “only” usually comes before.
**と = and, but only for nouns.** どようびとにちようび = Saturday and Sunday. と can't join two sentences — that needs the て-form in Unit 10.
**やすみ is a noun (day off, break); やすみます is a verb (to rest).** Japanese has many pairs like this, and the noun is usually the shorter one.
**ごぜん / ごご = a.m. / p.m.** They go **before** the hour: ごご3じ = 3 p.m. Japan uses the 24-hour clock on official timetables, but the 12-hour clock in conversation.

grammars.title: Hours and minutes
body: Hours = number + **[じ|ji]**. Minutes = number + **[ふん|fun]** or **[ぷん|pun]**. Most are regular; the irregular ones are in the table, and there are only a handful.
after: ⚠️ **The hours that break the pattern:** 4[時|ji] = **[よじ|yo-ji]** (not [よんじ|yonji]), 7[時|ji] = **[しちじ|shichi-ji]**, 9[時|ji] = **[くじ|ku-ji]** (not [きゅうじ|kyūji]). These three are the ones beginners mispronounce most.

**Rule of thumb for minutes:** numbers ending in 1, 3, 4, 6, 8, 10 take **[ぷん|pun]**; the rest take **[ふん|fun]**. The sounds merge because of the mouth, not because of grammar — say them aloud a few times and they'll stick.
**Full order:** [ごご|gogo] **3[じ|ji] 15[ふん|fun]** = 3:15 p.m. Hour first, then minutes, just as in English.

grammars.title: ～[から|kara]～[まで|made] — from … to …
body: **[から|kara]** = from (starting point). **[まで|made]** = until/to (end point). Both attach **after** the word they mark, not before — the most common pattern in Japanese, and you'll see it over and over.
Both work for **time** and **place**, and either can stand alone without its partner.

head: Sentence
Meaning
rows: [くじから|Ku-ji kara] [ごじまでです|go-ji made desu]。
[ジャカルタから|Jakaruta kara] [とうきょうまで|Tōkyō made]
[げつようびから|Getsuyōbi kara] [きんようびまで|kin'yōbi made]

after: **[から|kara] also means “because”** when it attaches to the end of a sentence rather than to a noun. Two different jobs for the same word; context almost always tells them apart.

dialogs.title: 会話 2 — Making plans
dialogs.intro: Budi and Ani set a time to meet. Notice the ます-form verbs starting to appear.

lines.speaker: ブディ:
lines.text: [アニさん|Ani-san]、[あした|ashita] [ひまですか|hima desu ka]。

lines.speaker: アニ:
lines.text: [あしたは|Ashita wa] [しごとが|shigoto ga] [あります|arimasu]。[あさってはひまです|Asatte wa hima desu]。
lines.id: Tomorrow I have work. The day after, I'm free.
lines.literal: tomorrow — as-for — work — [subject] — exists. day-after-tomorrow — as-for — free — is.

lines.speaker: ブディ:
lines.text: [あさっては|Asatte wa] [なんようびですか|nan-yōbi desu ka]。
lines.id: What day is the day after tomorrow?

lines.speaker: アニ:
lines.text: [すいようびです|Suiyōbi desu]。

lines.speaker: ブディ:
lines.text: [すいようびの|Suiyōbi no] [ごご|gogo] 2[じは|ji wa] [どうですか|dō desu ka]。
lines.literal: Wednesday — 's — afternoon — 2 — o'clock — as-for — how — is — [question]

lines.speaker: アニ:
lines.text: [すみません|Sumimasen]、2[じは|ji wa] [ちょっと|chotto]…。3[じは|ji wa] [だいじょうぶです|daijōbu desu]。
lines.id: Sorry, 2 is a bit… 3 o'clock is fine.
lines.literal: sorry, 2 — o'clock — as-for — a-little…. 3 — o'clock — as-for — all-right — is.

lines.speaker: ブディ:
lines.text: [じゃあ|Jā]、3[じに|ji ni] [あいましょう|aimashō]。[どこで|Doko de] [あいますか|aimasu ka]。
lines.id: Then let's meet at 3. Where shall we meet?
lines.literal: well-then, 3 — o'clock — at — let's-meet. where — at — meet — [question]

lines.speaker: アニ:
lines.text: [えきの|Eki no] [まえは|mae wa] [どうですか|dō desu ka]。
lines.id: How about in front of the station?

lines.speaker: ブディ:
lines.text: [いいですね|Ii desu ne]。[じゃあ|Jā]、[すいようびの|suiyōbi no] 3[じに|ji ni]。
lines.literal: good — is — isn't-it. well-then, Wednesday — 's — 3 — o'clock — at.

lines.speaker: アニ:
lines.text: [はい|Hai]、[またあさって|mata asatte]。
lines.id: OK, see you the day after tomorrow.

notes: **A trailing ちょっと… is a gentle refusal** — you saw it in Unit 2, and here its use is clear: turning down the suggested time without saying “I can't”. Japanese people rarely refuse bluntly, and an unfinished sentence is considered polite.
**に marks a specific time.** 3じ**に**あいましょう = let's meet **at** 3. The rule: use に when the time can be pointed to on a clock or calendar (hour, date, day), not for vague times (きょう, あした, いま, まいにち).
**～ましょう = “let's ～”.** The invitation form, fully explained in Unit 9. For now, just recognize it: あいます → あいましょう.
**ひま = free (not busy).** A な-adjective (Unit 7). Its opposite is いそがしい (busy).
**まえ = front.** えきのまえ = in front of the station. Position words are covered fully in Unit 5.
**なんようび = what day (of the week).** Don't confuse it with なんにち (what date).

grammars.title: The [ます|masu] form — polite verbs
body: Every Japanese verb has one polite form ending in **～[ます|masu]**. At A1 this is the form you use — safe with everyone, in every situation.
The good news: **the form never changes for the person doing the action.** No I/you/he, no singular/plural — no am/is/are, no -s. One form for everyone.

head: Form
Meaning
Example
rows: [やすみませんでした|yasumimasen deshita] — didn't rest
[やすみませんか|yasumimasen ka] — want to take a break?

after: **A single [ます|masu] form covers both now and later.** [いきます|ikimasu] can mean “I go” and “I will go”. Only the time word makes the difference: [あしたいきます|ashita ikimasu] = I'll go tomorrow.
⚠️ **The verb always comes at the end of the sentence.** No exceptions — which is why Japanese listeners often only learn what a sentence means at the very last second.

grammars.title: Days, and the time words around them
body: The names of the days all end in **[ようび|yōbi] ([曜日|yōbi])**, and their first part comes from the natural elements — moon, fire, water, wood, gold, earth, sun. The order matches Monday to Sunday exactly (Monday = moon day, as in English), so you only need to learn it once.
after: ⚠️ **Vague time words don't take [に|ni]**: [きょういきます|kyō ikimasu] (not [きょうにいきます|kyō ni ikimasu]), [まいにちべんきょうします|mainichi benkyō shimasu]. The ones that take [に|ni]: hours, dates, days, months — anything you can point to on a calendar.

blocks.text: Schedules in Japan are written in the same pattern everywhere, and once you recognize it, any sign with opening hours becomes readable:

head: What's written
Reading
Meaning
rows: [えいぎょうじかん|eigyō jikan] 営業時間
[くじから|ku-ji kara] [じゅうはちじまで|jūhachi-ji made]

blocks.title: Time is serious in Japan
items: A Japanese train counts as late if it's more than a minute behind, and passengers are given a delay certificate to show at work. This is not a joke.
Arriving **on time** means arriving **five minutes early**. Arriving on the exact minute already counts as cutting it close.
If you're going to be late, let people know before the time passes — not after. The phrase: **[すみません|Sumimasen]、10[ぷん|pun] [おくれます|okuremasu]。** (Sorry, I'll be 10 minutes late.)
